divergence: What if the Library of Alexandria never burned?

branches.title: Heliocentric Astronomy Taught Early
branches.summary: Preserved writings of Aristarchus let astronomers teach a Sun-centered system with supporting observations. Continuous copying and debate in the Library turned a fringe idea into standard teaching for navigators.
branches.scene: Students watch a brass Sun-centered orrery cast moving planetary shadows across the Library courtyard.
branches.reviewNote: Direct Aristarchus preservation; acceptance overstated but Antikythera-style orrery mechanically credible.

branches.title: Calculus Emerges From Archimedes
branches.summary: Complete copies of Archimedes' method of exhaustion survived, giving mathematicians tools for infinitesimals. Scholars in Samarkand built on them to develop early calculus for astronomy and architecture.
branches.scene: Mathematicians draw ever-finer polygons inside a circle on a sunlit observatory wall covered in chalk.
branches.reviewNote: Archimedean exhaustion to Islamic proto-calculus plausible; full calculus needs algebra notation.

branches.title: Anatomy Advances Circulation Knowledge
branches.summary: Surviving anatomical treatises from Herophilus and Erasistratus gave Salerno physicians detailed maps of nerves and blood vessels. Their translations spurred careful dissections and pulse studies centuries ahead of schedule.
branches.scene: A physician demonstrates blood flow using a glass model while students sketch its branching vessels.
branches.reviewNote: Alexandrian anatomy reaching Salerno plausible; glass model and circulation leap anachronistic.
